header.incumbent: Unnamed existing payments provider; its support was a ticket form.
header.tag_why: Halima chose the vendor that put named people and an on-call promise in the room, and dismissed our support tiers as 'a queue with a faster timer' despite our technical win with Ben.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For operations owners at high-stakes event buyers: 'A name, not a queue. A named solutions engineer and account lead, a shared channel, and someone who picks up on on-sale morning.' Lead with who answers when it breaks, not with tiers or response times.
messaging_changes.why: The decider dismissed our tiered support as 'a queue with a faster timer' and chose the vendor that offered named people and an on-call promise, in the words 'a name, not a queue' and 'someone who picks up'.

messaging_changes.change: Add an on-sale readiness plan as a proof point for ticketing and event buyers: a one-page, on-paper plan of what we do on an on-sale morning (who is on call, how the shared channel works, what happens at minute four if payments fail), paired with a named ticketing reference who can say who picked up. Offer it in the first meeting with the operations owner.
messaging_changes.why: The decider asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning, we had no such asset, and the rep admits it was buildable but offered logos instead.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For event and ticketing buyers, replace generic logos and stories with a named reference: 'Talk to [name] at [ticketing customer] about who picked up on their on-sale morning.' Put a person, not a logo wall, in front of the operations owner.
messaging_changes.why: The rep says 'I had logos. I didn't have a person', and the customer's language was about someone who picks up, which logos do not answer.

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: Stop leading with the developer and sandbox or load-test story when the economic decider is an operations owner. Keep it for the technical evaluator, and for the COO use: 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.' Answer what happens when it's down first.
messaging_changes.why: The load test won the CTO but drew only 'good.' from the decider, who said she does not buy uptime but what happens when it is down.

trigger.insight: The failure itself wasn't new (Ben said it had happened twice before). What changed was that the CEO saw it publicly, and the incumbent's silence during the outage was the sore point. The buying trigger was 'nobody helped us when it broke', not 'payments are unreliable'. That framed the whole evaluation around outage response from day one.
trigger.messaging: Open with the outage moment (minute four of an on-sale, who answers) instead of with platform capability.

decider.insight: Our champion was the CTO, but the decider was the COO, who owned the CEO-facing pain. Ben's preference was evidently not enough, and a one-meeting decision suggests Halima's criteria were set by the trigger, not by the technical evaluation. The rep's account shows we won the technical buyer and under-served the economic one.
decider.messaging: Build a separate COO/operations-owner track that answers 'what happens when it's down' rather than relying on the CTO to carry the case.

competitor.insight: The competitor won by showing up with the people, not by out-building us. The customer's questions shifted from technical to 'who' after that meeting. The rep's doubt that the competitor can actually staff every on-sale is unverified and irrelevant: the customer bought the promise and the faces. We don't know the competitor's name or whether the promise was kept.
competitor.messaging: Stop treating named people and on-sale coverage as a support-plan detail; make a named team and a shared channel visible in the first meeting.

decided.insight: The rep says the loss crystallized at Halima's sentence, but 'favourite' is the rep's own read and rested on Ben's confidence, not Halima's. The deal was likely already tilting once the competitor met her with named staff, and the rep only noticed when she said it out loud. The team planned an integration before the decider had signaled anything.
decided.messaging: Treat the champion's enthusiasm as unconfirmed until the economic decider has said what she needs, and have sales ask for her criteria early.

gaps.insight: The gap was a missing asset, not a missing product capability: an on-sale plan and a ticketing reference who could say who picked up. The rep admits it was buildable and chose not to, and the answer to 'why not' (the load test had won it) is a belief the customer's reaction didn't support. Logos (M8) were offered where a person was wanted.
gaps.messaging: Create an on-sale readiness plan template and a named ticketing reference, and use them in place of generic customer logos for high-stakes event buyers.

language.insight: The customer's vocabulary is about people and moments ('a name', 'someone who picks up', 'on-sale morning'), and the rep notes nobody said 'support'. Our words (support plans, tiers, response times, uptime history) sit in a different frame, and Halima's line explicitly rejects uptime as the thing she's buying. Two of the quotes aren't attributed to a named speaker.
language.messaging: Rewrite support copy in their terms, for example 'a named person who picks up on on-sale morning', and drop 'tiered response times' as the lead.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan directly what stopped them from asking the solutions engineer for a plan after Halima's request.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Ben, or check with the customer after the spring on-sales, whether the promise held.

close.rep_takeaway: Don't read a happy champion as a won deal: find out what the person who decides is actually buying, and when she asks for something on paper, build it that week instead of leaning on the demo that impressed the engineers.
